entries.title: Pocketbook Announces the Verta and Verta Color
entries.summary: The Pocketbook Verta and Pocketbook Verta Color e-readers are very affordable and will be released soon. The post Pocketbook Announces the Verta and Verta Color first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Pocketbook is gearing up to announce two new e-readers, available in the next couple of months. They are the Verta with an E-Ink Carta 1300 e-paper display and the Verta Color; these two devices will replace the Verse and Verse Color.

The Verta features a 6-inch E Ink Carta 1300 display with a resolution of 1,448 x 1,072 pixels at 300 PPI, which can display only 16 shades of gray. The Verta Color instead uses an E Ink Kaleido 3 panel that can also display 4,096 colors. The black-and-white e-paper display is 300 PPI, and the color display is 150 PPI. Both models have both a front-lit display and warm lighting.

Under the hood is a Rockchip RK3566 Quad-core ARM Cortex-A55 CPU running at 1.8 GHz, 1 GB of RAM, and 16 GB of internal storage. Bluetooth 5.0 supports audiobooks, and you can buy e-books from the PocketBook Store. Libby is preinstalled, and users can browse their local branch to borrow e-books, audiobooks, and digital magazines. A USB-C port is for transferring content and charging. The e-readers are powered by a 1,500 mAh battery, which lasts a couple of weeks of heavy use. Both of these e-readers are waterproof and rated IPX4.

Supported e-book formats include ACSM, CHM, DJVU, DOC, DOCX, EPUB, EPUB(DRM), FB2, FB2.ZIP, HTM, HTML, MOBI, PDF, PDF (DRM), PRC, RTF, TXT, AZW, CBR, AZW3, and CBZ.

The Verta will be available in many back-plate colors, such as black, white, red, and yellow. These are sold separately. It will retail for $169 when it comes out soon. The Verta Color will cost $179.99. That makes these devices affordable and cheaper than current-generation Kindle e-readers.

entries.content:
Looking for the best deals of the fall season? Prime Big Deal Days is Amazon’s annual two-day shopping event for Prime members, with exclusive savings across more than 35 categories—all with fast, free delivery. Looking for the best Kindle deals? Here is everything you need to know.

Amazon has put some of its previous-gen Kindles on sale ahead of Prime Big Deal Days, along with the Kindle Scribe and Kindle Scribe Colorsoft. Somehow, the Kindle Scribe without a front light still isn’t on sale, and it hasn’t gone on sale once since its release.

entries.title: Top 10 New Audiobooks for October 2026
entries.summary: New audiobooks for October 2026 include major anticipated releases like Partita by Barbara Kingsolver and Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus. The post Top 10 New Audiobooks for October 2026 first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Bram Stoker’s Dracula, adapted by Robyn Ahern and narrated by a full cast including Ella Purnell and Jonathan Bailey, stands out as the top audiobook pick for October 2026.

Threshing Day (Wing and Claw Collection)

The Threshing Day audiobook by Rebecca Yarros—part of the Empyrean universe's Wing and Claw Collection—was officially released on September 29, 2026. This special release features 13 standalone stories centering around beloved Fourth Wing characters (such as Xaden, Rhiannon, Dain, Liam, and more) as they navigate the brutal, high-stakes dragon-bonding trial at Basgiath War College.

The French Illusion: A Novel

The French Illusion audiobook by John Grisham was released on September 29, 2026. Marking a major departure from his classic courtroom dramas, this high-stakes release is Grisham's first-ever pure espionage thriller. The plot follows an American couple kidnapped during their honeymoon in Paris, pulling a young lawyer into an elaborate cross-border CIA operation to catch the culprits.

The Steps: A Memoir

The Steps audiobook by Sylvester Stallone was officially released on September 29, 2026. This powerful autobiography is narrated by Sylvester Stallone himself and features exclusive, original background music composed by legendary Rocky composer Bill Conti.

Miss Wolcott's Ghost: A Novel

Miss Wolcott’s Ghost audiobook by Louise Penny. It is scheduled for release on October 20, 2026. In an exciting development for fans, this 21st installment in the Chief Inspector Armand Gamache series is narrated by Alfred Molina—the acclaimed actor who previously portrayed Gamache in the Three Pines television adaptation.

A Court of Splintered Harmony

The A Court of Splintered Harmony audiobook by Sarah J. Maas—the highly anticipated sixth book in the A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) series—is officially scheduled for release on October 27, 2026.

Rules to Live By: How Extraordinary Lives Define What Really Matters

The Rules to Live By audiobook by professional climber, National Geographic photographer, and Academy Award–winning filmmaker Jimmy Chin was officially released on September 29, 2026.

Trust Fall

The Trust Fall audiobook by Lynn Painter was officially released on September 29, 2026. This rags-to-riches, opposites-attract romantic comedy is narrated by Saylor Bell Curda and Aidan Bissett.

Partita: A Novel

The Partita audiobook by Pulitzer Prize-winning author Barbara Kingsolver is officially scheduled for release tomorrow, October 6, 2026. This deeply moving novel is narrated by Megan Tusing.

Bram Stoker's Dracula

Audible presents Dracula, a brand-new, full-cast adaptation of Bram Stoker's masterpiece starring Ella Purnell, Jonathan Bailey, Aimee Lou Wood, Louis Partridge, David Jonsson, and Maggie Gyllenhaal.

entries.title: Pocketbook e-readers can now borrow magazines with Libby
entries.summary: A new software update for Pocketbook E-Readers has introduced digital magazine support for the Libby app. The post Pocketbook e-readers can now borrow magazines with Libby first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
PocketBook e-readers have had native Libby support for digital libraries. Users with newer models and older devices could browse their public library, borrow audiobooks and e-books, and read or listen to them on the PocketBook. The company just released the 6.11.1437 update, which now lets users borrow digital magazines through Libby-supported libraries.

The changelog states that “Magazines are now supported in the Libby app. Users can discover magazines in the library and search, borrow individual issues, and track what they’ve already checked out – all from a dedicated magazine page showing covers, issue details, and availability at a glance.”

Supported models include the Pocketbook Era, Pocketbook Verse Pro, and Pocketbook InkPad 4, along with existing models such as the Pocketbook Verse Pro Color, Pocketbook InkPad One, and Era Color. All of these e-readers are receiving the new software update.

The company also added automatic Bluetooth audio connection. The device now connects to a previously paired audio device automatically when it becomes available, when playback starts, or when Bluetooth is turned on, without any manual steps. If the connection drops, playback pauses and resumes automatically once reconnected, with a limited number of retry attempts.

Added the Send-to-Email feature to the Notepad application, allowing users to send notes directly from the device to one or multiple recipients, either as an attachment or in the email body, with PDF and TXT export options. Added an AI Selection function to the Notepad application, allowing users to simply circle handwritten text to instantly trigger handwriting recognition. They also added a Magic Shapes function to the Notepad application, automatically transforming rough hand-drawn circles, rectangles, arrows, and other shapes into clean geometric figures.

Bug fixes also include adjusting music or audiobook volume with headphone volume controls. Fixed an issue where audio playback did not resume correctly after the device automatically reconnected to Bluetooth headphones or a speaker.

Wrap up

Some e-readers let you borrow e-books from the public library. In the United States, you can visit your local branch’s website and use Send to Kindle. Kobo e-readers have OverDrive integration that only supports e-books, even though they all have an audiobook player; borrowing audiobooks is impossible.

Now that many PocketBook e-reader software platforms are mature enough, they are the only brand that supports e-books, audiobooks, and now digital magazines. Borrowing on a PocketBook is easy: simply attach your library card and four-digit PIN, and you can browse your local branch’s entire digital collection, borrow, and do everything on the e-reader without a computer or USB connection.

entries.title: Bigme F13 photo frame is AI Slop
entries.summary: Bigme has just entered the heavily saturated e-paper photo frame business. Is the F13 with E-Ink Spectra 6 a rare miss? The post Bigme F13 photo frame is AI Slop first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Bigme just released the F13, a 13.3 E-ink photo frame without an app to load your own content. Instead, it uses an AI voice assistant that will generate AI photos. The AI engine speaks broken English because it was designed for the Chinese market but is marketed worldwide. You would say things like “Hey Bigme, make an image about a goat playing basketball”, and it will. The images it generates are terrible quality and are all obviously AI-generated.

There are some saving graces; it comes preloaded with 1,000 world-famous paintings by famous artists. You can load additional content on an SD card and save images to it, and you can use the menu to load your own images, but the photo frame supports only a handful of image types. Not many people have a computer with an SD card reader, so you can’t rely on customers to do the work when they could buy the Bloomin8 photo frame, which has an excellent app for loading your own images wirelessly.

The Bigme F13 is a premium 13.3-inch smart E-Ink photo frame that uses advanced Spectra 6 technology to display rich, highly saturated, glare-free, print-quality visuals. It has a 1200×1600 resolution and 150 PPI. It has a microphone to access the Bigme AI assistant and a speaker so you can hear the AI voice. It is powered by a giant 18,000 mAh battery, which means you won’t have to charge it for over two years. It has a USB-C port for future charging.

Reviewers praise its sleek aluminum outer bezel and an innovative AI voice-to-image assistant that generates custom artwork on command, though some note that the companion app currently lacks a built-in content discovery library. Despite minor software and synchronization quirks, it serves as an excellent decorative centerpiece that can seamlessly pull double duty as a smart Google or Outlook calendar hub. It retails for $269.99 on the Bigme website.

entries.title: The Amazon Kindle Celebrates its 20th anniversary in 2027
entries.summary: Amazon plans to release special anniversary Kindle e-readers and revise its operating system for the 20th anniversary. The post The Amazon Kindle Celebrates its 20th anniversary in 2027 first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Amazon Kindle will celebrate its 20th anniversary in 2027, and the company will refresh its entire OS, make it easier to find the books you want to read, and make the UI more intuitive. Customers can also expect special anniversary editions of some Kindles.

According to a recent Wired article, “The Kindle business is booming. Amazon’s Kevin Keith, vice president of devices, says Kindles have seen double-digit growth over the last three years, with 2025 being the highest sales year in more than a decade. He says 60 to 65 percent of people buying new devices have never had a Kindle before, with Gen Z, millennials, and even Gen Alpha driving the lion’s share. This past January saw the highest single-month Kindle reading volume in history.

At the same time, Kindles are more expensive than ever. “Memory pricing is a little bit crazy,” Keith says, referring to the memory shortage behind the general price bump on all electronics. Amazon upped prices of existing Kindles earlier this year; the new devices match those prices.

More people are turning to both paper books and Kindles,” Green notes. “Is this a response to AI? It certainly seems that way—people are seeking out more genuine experiences in a time when authenticity feels scarce.” While surveys indicate that leisure reading overall is declining in the US, those who do read are purchasing more books than ever before.

entries.title: Onyx Boox Picco is sold out in the US
entries.summary: The Onyx Boox Picco is sold out in the USA, and pre-orders are no longer available. It remains to be seen when stock will be replenished. The post Onyx Boox Picco is sold out in the US first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Onyx BOOX started taking pre-orders for the Picco mini e-reader one week ago, and it is already sold out; customers can no longer pre-order the device. Onyx likely didn’t anticipate demand, and Hong Kong is the only market with stock. It remains to be seen if they will have to manufacture more, which will take a couple of months. Existing pre-orders will ship out sometime this month.

The Picco features a 3.97″ Monochrome Screen with a resolution of 480 x 800 and 235 PPI. It has both warm and cool lighting that you can switch with a button. Under the hood is an unknown processor, with a 16 GB Card Included, which is expandable to 2 TB. All data and e-books are stored on the card. It does not include a USB-C cable for data transfer. Instead, you have to use the BOOX Tiles app or the web. It has Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, runs on a 920 mAh battery, and measures 105.5 x 62 x 5.5 mm; it weighs 58 g.

The Picco supports EPUB, MOBI, AZW3, AZW, AZW5, FB2, FB2.ZIP, FB3, FBZ, TXT, PDB, PRC, RTF, HTML, XHTML, HTM, and CHM ebook formats. It includes a few apps, such as Pomodoro, Todo, and Countdown. The latest BOOX firmware formally confirms Boox’s partnership with Crosspoint, with the code now acknowledging that Crosspoint owns the core firmware. Boox is also officially listed as a partner on the Crosspoint homepage. That all said, the Boox Picco is still a fork of Crosspoint.

entries.title: Will you buy any of the new Kindle 2026 e-readers?
entries.summary: Would you pay more for 13th-generation Kindle e-readers, such as the Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft? The post Will you buy any of the new Kindle 2026 e-readers? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon surprised many people in the industry and customers worldwide when it announced a bevy of new Kindle e-readers. Instead of having just one model in each category, they now offer a couple. Some use the typical plastic, while others have an aluminum backing that makes them feel more premium. Some are available to order now, such as the base Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and the Paperwhite Signature Edition, while the two new Colorsoft units won’t ship until the end of October; the same goes for the new Kindle Clip and the cases with physical page-turn buttons.

Paperwhite

Amazon has just announced two new Kindle Paperwhite e-readers. Now thinner and lighter, with a 7-inch flush-front display, up to 12 weeks of battery life, adjustable warm light, and waterproofing. The Signature Edition adds aluminum, adaptive front lighting, 32GB of storage, and ad-free reading. Both will be available for purchase on October 28th 2026, with pre-orders happening right now.

The all-new Kindle Paperwhite is thinner and lighter than the previous lineup, waterproof, with an adjustable warm light for comfortable reading at any hour, and up to 12 weeks of battery life on a single charge. The Paperwhite display uses an oxide-thin film transistor backplane and is the largest Kindle Paperwhite display with the highest contrast ratio—delivering deep blacks and crisp text, and images that pop off the screen.

Both Kindle models have a resolution of 300 PPI. VoiceView screen reader, available over Bluetooth audio. : Supports 2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz networks with support for WEP, WPA, WPA2 and WPA3 security using password authentication. The dimensions are 26.8 mm x 174.7 mm x 6.8 mm

Available with 16GB of storage in Graphite starting at $199.99. Signature Edition with 32GB of storage is available in Graphite and Seaglass Green at $249.99.

Kindle Colorsoft 2026

Amazon just announced the Kindle Colorsoft e-reader, with a base model for $289 and a Signature Edition for $319 with an aluminum back plate. It has 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light, and double-tap page-turning. Both are available for purchase on October 28th 2026.

The new Kindle Colorsoft delivers paper-like color that’s easy on the eyes without the harsh glare of a tablet. Whether you’re scrolling through colorful covers in your library or flipping through a travel guide, comic, or graphic novel, the display makes color reading feel natural. To achieve paper-like color, our Kindle Colorsoft display includes a light guide with nitride LEDs to enhance color and increase brightness, all without washing out details. It uses an oxide backplane with custom waveforms for fast performance and higher contrast in both color and black-and-white content.

The latest Kindle Colorsoft has a completely redesigned display, using the reverse printing technology they applied across the lineup for edge-to-edge color. The light guide contains micro-deflectors that minimize stray light and improve uniformity, and an ultra-thin optical coating in the display stack improves clarity.

The Colorsoft Signature Edition adds aluminum housing, 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light, double-tap to

turn pages, and dock charging via pogo pins. Both models have a resolution of 300 PPI for black-and-white text and 150 PPI for Color. It supports the VoiceView screen reader, available over Bluetooth audio.

Kindle

The all-new 6-inch Kindle is the most pocket-sized Kindle they have ever made. With 16GB of storage, up to six weeks of battery life, and 30% faster book opening than the previous release, it is lighter and features a new seamless flush-front design. This required rethinking how the display, front light, and touch layers are assembled and bonded. They are also introducing edge-to-edge color across the entire family. The housing is made from recycled materials with a 100% recycled cobalt battery. Starting at $149.99 and available in Ube and Graphite.

This 6-inch Kindle is also available for the first time with an aluminum back—same pocket-sized form factor, same flush-front display, but with a premium feel you notice the moment you pick it up, and that younger readers are used to from reading on other devices. The housing is crafted from 80% recycled aluminum with a matte finish. Kindle in aluminum has 32GB of storage and is available in two colors, Alpine Sky Aluminum and Seaglass Green Aluminum.

Both Kindle models have 300 PPI resolution and support VoiceView screen reader, available over Bluetooth audio. Supports 2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz networks with support for WEP, WPA, WPA2, and WPA3 security using password authentication.

Wrap up

The new Kindle e-readers have increased in price since the previous generation’s price increase a month ago. It is hard to justify upgrading from the 12th generation to the 13th generation. However, the screen tech seems a bit refined. Aluminum gives them a slightly better design, and there are plenty of new covers.

Will you buy any of the new Kindle models, or will you instead buy the Kindle Clip, a wireless Bluetooth page-turn product designed by Amazon?

entries.title: Amazon Kindle Click is not shipping anytime soon
entries.summary: The Amazon Kindle Click release date has been pushed back for new orders, from November to March next year. The post Amazon Kindle Click is not shipping anytime soon first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Amazon Kindle Click is a new wireless Bluetooth page-turner, the first of its kind that Amazon developed itself. The company told Good e-Reader that, due to demand, the product won’t ship to people who ordered it on day 1 until November 11th 2026, and many orders have been pushed back to March 2027. The Amazon Kindle case with page-turn buttons has also been pushed back into next year.

Kindle Click costs $34.99 USD and $47 CAD and is available on all major Amazon websites. It has two big buttons: one to turn pages forward and the other to turn back. One of the most compelling features is the brightness controls to adjust the front-lit display and put the Kindle to sleep when you’re done.

Kindle Click comes in one color: white, and the buttons are grey. It comes with a lanyard to attach to your wrist, with a small hole for the attachment, but it is optional. A small battery powers it, and you charge it with a USB cable.

I don’t think Amazon anticipated how popular the Kindle Click would be and didn’t keep an adequate stockpile in the countries where it’s marketed, such as Canada, the UK, Japan, and the United States.

entries.title: Why Your E-Reader Sells a Different Bookstore in Every Country
entries.summary: It is tempting to read regional restrictions as the retailer being difficult The post Why Your E-Reader Sells a Different Bookstore in Every Country first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The same Kindle, the same account, the same title. Cross a border and the buy button disappears. Here is what is actually happening behind that message.

The message every traveling reader eventually sees

Anyone who has owned a Kindle or a Kobo for more than a year has probably met it: “Due to copyright restrictions, the Kindle title you are trying to purchase is not available in your country.” On Kobo the wording is softer, the title simply fails to appear in search, or shows up with no price attached. On Libby, the library card that worked at home stops returning results the moment the app decides you are somewhere else.

None of this is a bug. It is the visible edge of a licensing system that predates e-readers by decades, and that the devices themselves inherited without much modification. Understanding it explains a lot of otherwise baffling behavior, from the regional catalog mismatch between amazon.com and amazon.co.uk to why a Tolino bought in Germany behaves nothing like the same hardware sold in Italy.

Books are licensed by territory, not by language

When an author signs with a publisher, the contract rarely grants “world rights.” English-language rights are commonly split three ways: North America, the United Kingdom and Commonwealth, and everything else. A different publisher can hold each slice. A Canadian imprint might have the print edition but not the ebook. A UK house might have the ebook but only for markets outside the US.

Retailers then have to enforce these boundaries at the point of sale. Amazon, Kobo, Apple Books and Google Play all receive metadata from publishers that lists the countries in which a given edition may be sold. If your account is registered in a country that is not on that list, the edition is hidden or blocked. The territorial rights model is why two customers sitting side by side on the same Wi-Fi network can see different prices, different covers, or different availability for a single ISBN.

Self-published titles tend to be the exception. An author uploading directly through KDP or Kobo Writing Life usually keeps world rights and ticks every territory, which is why indie catalogs feel more consistent across borders than traditional ones.

How the store decides where you are

This is where e-readers differ from, say, a streaming app on a phone. A dedicated reading device makes very few network requests, and most of them are to a single vendor. So the store leans less on your current IP address and more on account metadata.

On Kindle, the deciding factor is the “Country/Region” setting under Manage Your Content and Devices, which Amazon ties to a billing address and a payment method. Kobo binds the account to the country selected at signup and to the local partner store (Indigo in Canada, Rakuten in Japan, Fnac in France, Walmart in the US). Libby and OverDrive check library card eligibility, which in most public systems requires proof of residency in a specific municipality or county.

IP location still plays a part, though. Amazon compares the country of your connection against the country on file, and enough mismatches will prompt a request to update the address. Kobo’s web store redirects to a regional domain based on IP before you ever sign in. The broader mechanics of how services fingerprint a visitor’s location, and what changes when that signal is masked, are laid out in Gizmodo’s explainer on how location-based content restrictions work, which is useful background for anyone trying to work out whether an ebook problem is an account issue or a network one.

What the regulators actually decided

Readers in Europe often assume this kind of restriction was outlawed years ago. The rule they are thinking of is the EU geo-blocking regulation, which banned retailers from redirecting or refusing customers based on their member state. But the text carves out copyright-protected digital content by name. Ebooks, along with music, software and video, sit outside the ban on differential access. The retailer must let you see the site, but it does not have to sell you the book. The full text of Regulation (EU) 2018/302 spells this out in Article 4, and a scheduled review in 2020 left the exemption in place.

The reasoning offered at the time was that removing the exemption would collapse territorial licensing and, in countries with fixed book price laws such as France and Germany, undermine the pricing regime that keeps independent bookshops alive. Whether that logic holds for digital files is a debate the industry has yet to settle.

The practical fallout on the device

A few consequences follow directly from all this, and they explain some of the stranger support threads on any e-reader forum.

Purchased books travel with you. Rights are checked at the time of sale, not at the time of reading. A title bought while the account was set to the US remains readable after moving to Spain, even if it is no longer purchasable there. The library is not retroactively pruned.

Changing your account country is a real change, not a cosmetic one. On Kindle it can wipe your Kindle Unlimited subscription, alter what is eligible for Prime Reading, and reset the store to a currency that may not match your card. Amazon also requires a local payment method for some regions. On Kobo, switching countries can orphan a partner-store account entirely.

Library apps are the strictest of all. Because Libby and OverDrive licenses are negotiated per library system, not per publisher, there is no account setting to change. Eligibility is whatever the card allows, and many systems now verify address at renewal.

Sideloading bypasses the store but not the DRM. An EPUB bought from a regional store still carries Adobe or Kobo DRM tied to the account that bought it. A DRM-free EPUB, which is what most small presses and technical publishers sell, moves between devices and countries with no restriction whatsoever. This is the strongest argument for buying DRM-free where it is available.

What to check before assuming the catalog is broken

When a title refuses to appear or to sell, the order of diagnosis is fairly consistent. Confirm the account country in the store’s settings, since a stale address from a previous move is the single most common cause. Then check whether the edition exists at all in your region by searching the retailer’s local domain from a browser rather than from the device, which has a much smaller search interface. Then look at the publisher listed on the product page; if it is an imprint you associate with a different market, the edition is probably not licensed where you are.

Only after those three steps does the connection itself become a suspect. E-readers cache location decisions aggressively, and a device that made its first store request from a hotel abroad may keep serving that region until it is deregistered and set up again.

The catalog is a map of contracts, not a map of the world

It is tempting to read regional restrictions as the retailer being difficult. In most cases the retailer would rather sell the book. What the device is showing you is the shape of a rights agreement negotiated between an author, an agent and a handful of publishers, often years before the ebook edition existed. The hardware simply renders it. Knowing that will not make the buy button reappear, but it does make the next “not available in your country” message a great deal easier to interpret.
